title: Elmore Leonard's 10 Rules of Writing
rule: Carry dialogue with 'said' only; no adverbs on 'said'. The line belongs to the character; any other verb or adverb is the writer intruding and breaks the rhythm.
example: Leonard: 'grumbled, gasped, cautioned, lied' are intrusive; 'he admonished gravely' is the mortal sin.

title: Elmore Leonard's 10 Rules of Writing
rule: Dialect sparingly: do not spell speech phonetically or fill the page with apostrophes; catch speech by rhythm and word choice. Avoid detailed character description; let how they speak identify them. Cut what readers skip (readers rarely skip dialogue). Closing test: 'If it sounds like writing, I rewrite it.'
example: Hemingway 'Hills Like White Elephants': only physical detail is the woman taking off her hat, yet we know who they are from how they speak; no adverbs.

title: What is 'On the Nose' Dialogue?
rule: On-the-nose = characters say exactly what they think, feel or intend. Fix: speak around the feeling, via action/reaction, indirection, subject changes, unfinished thoughts. Blunt truths are allowed only if earned by the scene.
example: On the nose: 'I am very angry with you right now.' Subtext: 'It's funny how you always know what to say to ruin my day.'

title: On the nose / McKee via secondary sources (web search summary)
rule: McKee (via secondary quotes, not the book): on-the-nose writing leaves nothing for the actor/reader to do; subtext is the unspoken inner life and audiences look past the words for it. Fix: keep the hidden meaning, change the surface line. Final Draft dissents that on-the-nose is not always bad.
example: 'Subtext is the stuff of acting. On the nose writing leaves nothing for the actors to do.' (unverified against McKee's Dialogue p.46)

title: Cover the Character Names (MovieMaker)
rule: Cover-the-names test: hide speaker names over the dialogue; if you cannot tell who is speaking, the voices are not distinct. Industry readers use it.
example: 'If you find yourself confused and unsure of which character is saying what, there's a problem.'

title: Voice ledger (bookwriter.vip blog)
rule: LLM characters converge on a safe neutral narrator voice unless each character's speech profile is persisted in context and loaded when they speak. Fields: cadence, vocabulary register, sentence-length patterns, hesitations, regional markers, signature phrases, things the character would never say, distance between inner and spoken voice.
example: 'Characters collapse into one another by chapter four.' (vendor blog; opinion, not measured)

title: The AI dialogue trap (Wayline)
rule: Named LLM dialogue failures: homogenized voices; unnatural smoothness (no interruptions, fragments, tangents); predictability; out-of-character register; flat sarcasm/irony/understatement; shallow emotional range. Fix: define the emotional beat and voice first, then reintroduce fragments and quirks; hand-write subtext-heavy scenes.
example: 'a stoic, battle-hardened warrior suddenly spouting flowery prose'; AI dialogue 'unnervingly smooth and devoid of these quirks'. General claims, no measurement.

title: What AI fundamentally misunderstands (SleuthSayers, Brian Thornton)
rule: Fiction tells of LLM prose: corrective reframe ('not because X but because Y'); fragmented twist sentence; emotional labeling; standalone wisdom-summary line closing a scene; over-varied dialogue tags (murmured, breathed, exhaled, rasped); sensory cataloguing; reflective gerund openers.
example: 'A wave of grief washed over her'; 'Some wounds, she understood now, never fully closed'; 'She smiled at him: not with kindness. With liberation.'

title: ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny! (Jentzsch & Kersting)
rule: Measured: over 90% of 1008 ChatGPT-generated jokes were the same 25 jokes (memorised, not newly generated); it explains valid jokes but also invents explanations for invalid ones; joke-like surface features mislead it. Implication: ask for jokes from this world's specifics, never 'a joke'.
example: Abstract: 'Over 90% of 1008 generated jokes were the same 25 Jokes.' (GPT-3.5-era; may not hold for newer models)

title: Qwen3 humour scaling (Agrawal & Mamidi, CHum 2026) via search summary
rule: Automated LLM judges rank larger models funnier, but human annotators found no significant aggregate difference; judge shows position and length bias. Do not use an LLM as the funniness gate.
example: Five Qwen3 variants; human vs automated rating disagreement (summary only, paper not opened).

title: John Vorhaus comedy writing tools
rule: Rule of three: two beats set a pattern, the third breaks it (deflating, not escalating). Inappropriate response: drop an off-register reaction into a situation with a narrow appropriate range. Comic opposites: give each character one rule, give another the opposite rule, lock them together.
example: Doctor lists 'a brain tumor, heart disease, and a really ugly tie'; passenger in a car chase worries about 'my fuel economy'.

title: The rule of three (GPTZero)
rule: LLMs default to triplet lists ('x, y, and z') regardless of content; a single triplet is harmless, a pattern is a fingerprint. No measured frequency data in the source; also 'not X but Y' is widely called the hardest tic to shake (Atlantic, via AI Weekly summary, not opened). Use three only when the third item earns a break.
example: 'address bias challenges, improve its performance, and expand its applications.'

title: GDC 08: Portal creators on writing (Shacknews)
rule: Portal: dialogue earns its place by doing design work (hints, attaching players to the companion cube); writing was shaped by playtests and cost constraints; comedy is hard: 'unpleasant, funny dialog is funny to the writer once, maybe'. Wolpaw (web summaries, not in this article): player silent as straight man in a mad world; Wheatley is a frantic offset to GLaDOS's slow delivery (contrast pairs).
example: Wolpaw: 'If you're writing a funny game, first of all, god help you.'

title: Pratchett interview (L-Space)
rule: Humour serves the story; position is timing: the footnote is a delayed drop because the reader's eye must travel down the page. Tampere dissertation (snippet only) lists his devices: paraprosdokian, bathos, running gags, comic footnotes, reversal.
example: Pratchett: 'So I use the footnote as a delayed drop.' ... 'That's timing.'

title: Spaceplan (search summaries of reviews)
rule: Spaceplan: absurd premise played straight (a ship powered by potatoes) plus a snarky AI narrator doing all the talking; reviewers call it funny but short. 'Deadpan' is my inference, not a reviewer label. No craft analysis found; a null for how it is written.
example: Puns 'probetato', 'spudnik'; premise 'a total misunderstanding of A Brief History of Time'.
